## Eight assumptions practitioners hold, and their negations

| # | Usual assumption | Negation and the conditional effect it implies |
|---|---|---|
| A1 | Stacked convs compound, so an upstream conv makes a downstream conv more valuable. | The receptive field saturates, so a 3x3 conv on edge 2 or 4 gains less when edge 0 is already a 3x3 conv. |
| A2 | Parallel routes into one node add capacity. | They substitute for each other, so a conv added next to a conv on the same fan-in loses value. |
| A3 | Skip connections are harmless and complementary to convs. | Skip on a sibling edge supplies the identity or refinement path, so a conv on a sibling or downstream edge gains more or less depending on the mechanism, and the sign is not fixed. |
| A4 | Avg-pool is a neutral, cheap op. | Pooling blurs features, so a conv after it works on degraded input, while a skip beside it restores sharp information. |
| A5 | The direct input-to-output edge is just a shortcut. | It acts as a capacity supplier, so convs on the chain matter less when it is a 3x3 conv. |
| A6 | 3x3 is better than 1x1 everywhere. | After an upstream 3x3, a 1x1 downstream adds channel mixing without more blur, so the relative value of 1x1 rises. |
| A7 | Downstream convs always profit from upstream feature quality. | A downstream conv already present makes an upstream upgrade redundant. |
| A8 | Interactions reflect only graph connectivity. | The op type of the parallel or upstream edge matters beyond connectivity: pool, skip and conv parents each change the gain differently. |

Each hypothesis below comes from one of these negations. Every condition links two different edges, none makes the edited edge inert, and no condition setting appears more than twice.
